messages.subject: Post-doc/research associate opportunity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I am looking for a post-doc or research associate for working ~2years with me at the University of Calgary, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, on a number of projects. I am looking for a bit of a unicorn... ideally someone:
- very comfortable with advanced Bayesian hierarchical models, including SCR and derivatives (comfortable with integration of GPS collar and camera trap data), Occupancy models, Integrated Pop Model, etc... applications would include
* feral pig research in Canada
* rodent ecology in agricultural land in Canada
- also comfortable and proficient with basic analysis and modeling with GLM/GLMM... specific applications would involve analysis of fairly standard epidemiological study on antimicrobial resistance in poultry in Indonesia...I know, a bit of an odd mix, but that's where the funding is coming from.

Looking for someone ASAP, so if that sounds like you, get in touch!
Thanks!
Mathieu Pruvot
University of Calgary

messages.subject: Help with Figure 8.12, AHM2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Apologies in advance if these questions have been answered before on the forum, I'm not seeing them... I would value anyone's input on the below.

Background
I'm going through the examples in AHM2 Chapter 8 Interactions Among Species. More specifically, I'm working on the model by Waddle et al. (2010), as described in section 8.3.2. I've used my own data which has two felids, large and medium sized. The larger felid being dominant over the smaller one. Data is from approx. 700 camera trap sites at eleven nature reserves which were active at different times of the year. These reserves are located quite far from each other and thus the terrain, habitat, climate, etc. differs somewhat.

Methods
As an initial experimental phase I've included all the covariates I have available which might influence the two species' probability of site use. These include: NDVI, elevation, rainfall, terrain ruggedness, distance to water, human footprint index, and temperature. Some of the results show these covariates having an influence on species prob. of site use while for others the beta coefficients overlap zero.

Question 1
I would like to plot the relationship between occupancy and the covariates for the subordinate species with and without the presence of the dominant species.  I realise this might be a stupid question... But, in the book's example, why is 500 subtracted from the original prediction values and then divided by 100. Please see the code in blue in the snippet below (code from AHM2 to create figure 8.12, page 495).

# Predictions of elevation profile of occupancy
epred.orig <- 200:1000     # Approximate elevation range in data
epred <- (epred.orig - 500) / 100
op <- par(mfrow = c(1,2), mar = c(5,5,4,3), cex.lab = 1.5, cex.axis = 1.5)
plot(epred.orig, plogis(qlogis(tmp$mean.psiB[1]) + tmp$beta1B[1] * epred),
    type = 'l', lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = 'red', frame = FALSE,
    xlab = 'Elevation (metres)', ylab = 'Predicted occupancy prob. of BTNW',
    ylim = c(0,1))
lines(epred.orig, plogis(qlogis(tmp$mean.psiB[2]) + tmp$beta1B[2] * epred),
    type = 'l', lwd = 3, col = 'blue')

Question 2
What should I use for the part "(xxx.orig - 500)/100" when plotting the relationship between covariates and occupancy in my own model? It makes sense to me to set range of values for the covariate in the first line of code above. But what should one do with the second line of code? I can see that the plot changes quite a lot if I change "500" or "100" to something else.

Thank you kindly!

messages.subject: One-year postdoc (modeling wildlife survey data) at the Leibniz-IZW Berlin (start: Nov 1, 2023)
messages.subject_clean: One-year postdoc (modeling wildlife survey data) at the Leibniz-IZW Berlin (start: Nov 1, 2023)
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone;

We - the team Biodiversity Dynamics in the Department of Ecological Dynamics at the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research in Berlin (ecodynizw.github.io/team-biodiversity.html <https://ecodynizw.github.io/team-biodiversity.html>) - are looking for a one-year post-doc (90%), starting November 1, 2023.

This position will focus on the development and application of modern approaches to process and analyse wildlife survey data. One component of the work will be to analyse camera-trapping and SMART patrol data using a (community) occupancy framework. Further work includes the co-development of an R Shiny App to make the analytical approaches available to a broader scientific and conservation community, and the co-development of AI (convolutional neural network) approaches to locate and classify animals in camera-trap images. This project represents a pilot phase with good chances of receiving additional funding; the postdoc will be involved in developing a proposal for continuation of the project.

The deadline for applying online is September 17th, 2023.

For more information on the position and how to apply, please visit: https://leibniz-institutfuerzoo-undwildtierforschung.softgarden.io/job/34929244?l=de

Please forward this email to students and colleagues who might be interested.

Thank you!

Rahel

messages.subject: Call for hosting the International Statistical Ecology Conference (ISEC) in 2026
messages.subject_clean: Call for hosting the International Statistical Ecology Conference (ISEC) in 2026
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues (apologies for cross-posting),

We are inviting expressions of interest to host the International Statistical Ecology Conference (ISEC) in 2026. ISEC is organised every two years (typically in June or July), and it has been a very successful event to build connections across the statistical ecology community all over the world. For information about the last ISEC, held in Cape Town in 2022, please see https://www.isec2022.org/.

ISEC 2026 will be the 10th iteration of the conference, and it has been customary for past organisers to provide some guidance to prospective hosts. Conference hosts can also apply for financial support from the ISEC Foundation.

Please fill out this form to let us know that you are interested in hosting ISEC 2026: https://forms.office.com/r/8nrRGESPPL. We would like to receive applications by November 30, 2023. If you have any questions, or would like to discuss anything, you can contact the chair of the long-term planning committee (Brett McClintock, isec...@gmail.com).

We hope to see many of you in Swansea for ISEC 2024.

Best wishes,
ISEC long-term planning committee

messages.subject: posterior samples - negative binomial model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working on modeling the effects of climate and landscape on mosquito abundance. Right now, I am working on a model to explore how the wind speed affects the trap effectiveness, with the idea of incorporating this effect into the final model.

I am using jagsUI, and mostly following examples in the AHM books and adapting them to my case study. However, I have little expertise in Bayesian statistics and I am finding some problems in carrying on model checking.

My most basic model right now looks like this:

model{
#likelihood
for (i in 1:N){
  captures[i] ~ dnegbin(p[i], r)
  p[i] <- r/(r+lambda[i])
  log(lambda[i]) <-  alpha[week_num[i]] + beta1*wind2[i]

}
#random effect
for(j in 1:M){
  alpha[j] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha, tau.alpha) # Mean and precision = 1/variance
}

#priors
beta1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
mu.alpha~dnorm(0, 0.001)
tau.alpha ~ dgamma(1.0E-3, 1.0E-3)
sigma.alpha <- sqrt(1/tau.alpha)
r ~ dunif(0,50)
}

Some colleagues recommended sampling from the posterior distribution of the model’s parameter and developing simulated data to visually compare is they are similar to the observed data or not, as a part of model checking and fit assessment. For this, I thought of doing something similar to AHM Book1 5.9:

# Likelihood of the model
for (i in 1:M){
Cmax[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) # note no variance parameter
log(lambda[i]) <- alpha[facFor[i]] + beta[facFor[i]] * elev[i]
resi[i] <- (Cmax[i]-lambda[i]) / (sqrt(lambda[i])+e) # Pearson residual
}

#simulated data
lambda2 <- array(dim = c(15000, 267))
for(j in 1:267){ # Loop over sites
lambda2[,j] <- exp(out5$sims.list$alpha[,facFor[j]] +
out5$sims.list$beta[,facFor[j]] * elev[j]) # linear regression/backtransform
}

However, I do not understand if this would be correct for a negative binomial distribution.

I also noticed that for some fit assessment approaches it is necessary to add a simulated data set like captures.new <http://captures.new>[i] ~ dnegbin(p[I], r) on the model itself. In this case, are we doing the same as in the previous example?

I also thought about using a test statistic to complement the GoF assessment, but I am not sure how I should choose between different options. For example, I have found mixed opinions on whether the Chi-square test statistic would be appropriate or not for a negative binomial distribution.

My apologies if this post results are too beginner-level for this group, but I have been struggling for some time with the model assessment. I would appreciate it if anyone could give me some advice regarding this issue or recommend any bibliography, website or post on the subject.

Cheers,
Sonia.
